segments.say: Think about the happiest people you can imagine. What do their lives look like? For many of us, the picture is full of fireworks. Big trips, big parties, big moments of joy that light up the sky. The happiest life, we assume, must be the one with the most intense highs. It's a very natural idea. And it's our next myth.

show.title: The myth of the big highs

segments.say: Nora's brightest moment with the window came on her very first night. She sat on the floor among the boxes, a sandwich in her lap, and watched the sun go down over the water. It was almost too beautiful. She remembers thinking, this is it, this is what happiness feels like. And for a while afterwards, she measured every evening against that one.

In 1991, the psychologist Ed Diener and his colleagues Ed Sandvik and William Pavot published a chapter with a title that says it all. Happiness is the frequency, not the intensity, of positive versus negative feelings. It appeared in a book on subjective well-being, and it gathered evidence from studies in which people reported on their feelings, often again and again over many days.

show.who: Ed Diener, Ed Sandvik and William Pavot
show.what: Happiness is the frequency, not the intensity, of positive feelings

segments.say: What they found was quietly radical. How often people felt good was a much better guide to their overall well-being than how intensely they felt good. People who were happy most of the time, in a mild and steady way, were the ones who described themselves as happy overall. The dazzling peaks added surprisingly little.

show.title: What they found
items: How often you feel good predicts well-being best
How intensely you feel good adds much less
Small, frequent pleasures beat rare, dazzling ones

segments.say: Diener and his colleagues also pointed to a reason why intense highs may not help as much as we'd think. Intense positive moments are rare. And when you've just had one, the ordinary days that follow can look a little grey beside it. A very bright light makes everything around it seem darker. The high doesn't just fade. It can quietly lower the shine of what comes next.

That was exactly Nora's problem. After that first glowing night, the ordinary evenings, with cloud over the water or rain on the glass, felt like a disappointment. Not because they were bad, but because she kept holding them up against the best evening of all. Her happiness hadn't vanished. It had been outshone by a memory.

And yet, look at an evening like this one. A grey sea, a cup of tea, a little rain on the window. Nothing glittering. Nothing to post or to tell anyone about. But if the research is right, it's evenings like this, many of them, gently pleasant, that make up most of a happy life.

There's a second half to this myth, and it's about memory. Because the way we remember good and bad experiences is not the way we lived them. Our memories keep some moments and quietly drop others. And one of the most famous demonstrations of this involves a bowl of very cold water.

In 1993, Daniel Kahneman, Barbara Fredrickson, Charles Schreiber and Donald Redelmeier published a study in Psychological Science. Volunteers held one hand in cold water, which is uncomfortable but harmless. It became known as the cold hand study, and it showed something about memory that almost nobody expected.

show.what: When more pain is preferred to less

segments.say: In one trial, a hand went into water at fourteen degrees Celsius for sixty seconds. In another trial, the hand stayed in the same cold water for sixty seconds, and then for an extra thirty seconds while the water was warmed by about one degree. Still cold, just a little less so. So the second trial contained all of the first one's discomfort, plus more.

show.title: Cold water trial
show.label: for 60 seconds, then an extra 30 seconds slightly warmer

segments.say: Then the volunteers were asked which of the two trials they would rather repeat. Logically, the shorter one should win. It had less discomfort in total. But most of the volunteers chose to repeat the longer trial. The one with more cold, but a gentler ending. Their memory of the experience had been shaped not by its total, but by how it ended.

This pattern is called the peak end rule. When we look back on an experience, our memory tends to lean on two moments in particular. The most intense moment, the peak. And the final moment, the end. How long the experience lasted matters surprisingly little. Kahneman called that last part duration neglect.

show.title: The peak-end rule
items: Memory leans on the most intense moment
Memory leans on the final moment

segments.say: You may recognise this from your own life. A holiday that's remembered mostly by its last day, good or bad. A film that's judged almost entirely by its final scene. A lovely evening that feels a little spoiled, in memory, because of one sharp word just before everyone went home. The middle was fine. But the ending wrote the story.

show.title: You may know this feeling
items: A holiday remembered by its last day
A film judged by its final scene
An evening coloured by how it ended

segments.say: The same idea was later studied with real medical procedures. In 1996, Donald Redelmeier and Daniel Kahneman published a study in the journal Pain, in which patients rated their discomfort moment by moment during a colonoscopy. Afterwards, their overall memory of the procedure was linked to the worst moment and to the last few minutes, far more than to how long it had lasted.
And this strange way of remembering doesn't only apply to short experiences. It can even shape how we judge a whole life.

In 2001, Ed Diener, Derrick Wirtz and Shigehiro Oishi published a study they called the James Dean effect, after the young film star whose life ended suddenly at its height. People read short descriptions of imaginary lives. Some lives were wonderful, and ended suddenly. Others were the same wonderful life, with a few extra years that were pleasant, but a little less wonderful, added at the end.

show.who: Ed Diener, Derrick Wirtz and Shigehiro Oishi
show.what: End effects of rated life quality

segments.say: And people tended to rate the shorter, purely wonderful life as more desirable than the same life with some extra, mildly pleasant years. Logically, those extra years were still good years. Adding them should have made the life better, not worse. But the ending coloured the whole. It's as if we judge a life the way we judge a story, by its final chapter, rather than adding up every good day along the way. And the same quiet bias seems to shape how we look back on a summer, a friendship, or a year in a new home.

So here's how these two ideas fit together. In daily life, it's the frequent, gentle pleasures that seem to matter most. But in memory, it's the peaks and the endings. Nora's first night by the window became a peak, and her mind kept comparing everything to it. That's a natural trick of memory. It just isn't a fair picture of her life.

There are some gentle lessons here. Look for small pleasures that can happen often, rather than waiting for rare spectacular ones. Try not to let one bright peak outshine every ordinary day. And when you can, give good experiences a good ending. A slow last walk at the end of a holiday, a warm goodbye, a quiet cup of tea at the end of an evening.

show.title: Gentle lessons
items: Don't let one peak outshine every ordinary day
Give good experiences a good ending

segments.say: So Nora began to give her own evenings a better ending. Nothing grand. Just a few quiet minutes by the window before bed, with the lamp turned low, looking out at whatever the sea happened to be doing. Sometimes it was silver. Sometimes it was black, with a single light far out on the water. She stopped asking whether it was as beautiful as that first night. She simply let each evening end gently, and found that the days began to feel kinder in memory.

show.sub: A few minutes by the glass

segments.say: But if frequent, gentle pleasures are what matter, there's still a problem. Frequent pleasures fade fastest of all. The more often we do something nice, the more ordinary it becomes. So is there any way to keep a good thing feeling fresh? Surprisingly, the answer may involve doing something most of us would never choose. Interrupting it.
